    #163073. Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1916 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your tech giant.
    • Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit.
    • Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your tech giant. Right now. Or else.

    Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”.

    Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”.

    Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”.

    Industry observers note that president Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

    According to recent reports, fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

    It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official claims. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”.

    Industry observers note that documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

    “The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

    “It’s just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what’s best for the company in the short or long term, what’s best for shareholders, but what’s best for politics and what the government is demanding.”.

    According to recent reports, “That’s not what you want from any organization,” he adds. “When you’re talking about the world’s most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that’s a huge problem.”.

    According to recent reports, representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

    The parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the company’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office.

    During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research.

    Sources indicate that at the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, indicates the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times.) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “a horrible, horrible thing.” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration mentioned it was renegotiating the deals.

    Sources indicate that the same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s new CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing’s military. Tan’s former firm, Cadence Design Systems, pleaded guilty to violating US sanctions by selling semiconductor designs to a restricted Chinese military university, and agreed to pay more than $140 million in fines. Tan was never personally charged, but the violations happened while he was the CEO.

    Two weeks later, the president was watching Maria Bartiromo’s show on the Fox Business Network. It mentioned a letter a senator had sent Intel about the China ties. Trump posted, “The CEO of INTEL is highly CONFLICTED and must resign, immediately. There is no other solution to this problem.”.

    Sources indicate that tan went to the Oval Office on August 11 to see if there was, in fact, another solution. He got 40 minutes with the president, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

    Tan claimed his experience in China was a strength, not a detriment. According to the book Regime Change, Tan argued that there was no way he could’ve known about every one of the deals his many companies made; Trump, who had his own sprawling business empire, surely knew what that was like. Tan promised to give up his holdings in China, according to a letter Tan shared with Intel’s board, and put any proceeds into a blind trust.

    In a recent development, “The primary goal was to eliminate any worries about Lip-Bu himself, his Cadence background, and his investments with China,” according to a source with knowledge of the matter. But there were major financial concerns for Intel, too. “We had declining revenues and needed money.”.

    In a recent development, neither Tan’s letter, excerpted in the complaint, nor Trump’s social media posts praising the CEO after the meeting mentioned anything about giving the government a chunk of the firm. Yet Trump later insisted that a deal had been cooked up right then and there. “He came in, he saw me, we talked for a while. I liked him a lot, I thought he was very good,” the president told The Wall Street Journal. “I stated, ‘You know what? I think the United States should be given 10% of Intel.’ And he said, ‘I would consider that.’”.

    “I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy,” Trump later recalled.

    Recent findings suggest that according to the court filing’s review of Intel’s internal documents, Shapiro—a former partner at the Newly introduced York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—made a verbal offer on August 18. Ultimately, in exchange for the cut of Intel, the Trump administration would free up the $8.9 billion US government grants that it had already won. They wanted about a tenth of the firm’s stock for free, in exchange for Washington keeping the commitment it had already made.

    In a recent development, then came the call in which Shapiro insisted there was no room for negotiation. “The board needs to consider,” he said, according to Intel’s summary of his remarks included in the court documents, the “benefits of having a friend in this administration and what the administration can do to help Intel (including with customers).”.

    Intel’s board met, and decided they hated the deal. “The economic terms that had been proposed [by] the Administration were not, in their current form, attractive to the tech giant,” minutes of the meeting, reprinted in the lawsuit, noted.

    It has been revealed that but they went ahead with it anyway. Paisner’s lawyers say in the court documents the board took the offer thrust forward by the administration. Intel’s attorneys disagree, arguing in their motion to dismiss that there was some back-and-forth deal-making, and it made the agreement more favorable to the firm. The grants became “immediately available” while “strategically aligning the interests of Intel’s stockholders and the US Government.”.

    On August 25, Lutnick released a video with Tan, sitting side-by-side on cushioned chairs. “I really look forward to have the US government be my shareholder,” Tan turned to Lutnick and stated. “And we can work together and make Intel great again.”.

    It has been revealed that inside the company, the video was “a surprise to everyone,” according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. Some employees joked that it was reminiscent of a “hostage video.”.

    Not long after that, Nvidia—led by Tan’s friend Jensen Huang—made a $5 billion investment in Intel. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted. “Who would not want to make deals like that?”.

    Deals, plural. On the day Tan was hauled to the Oval Office, Trump announced that his administration had been negotiating separately with Huang. The Nvidia leader was beyond eager to sell more of his semiconductors to China. “And I said, if I’m going to do that, I want you to pay us as a country something,’” Trump said. They settled on 15 percent of all sales of the H20 model chip. Months after that, they cut a second deal: a 25 percent bounty on sales of Nvidia’s even-more advanced H200 chips.

    In their lawsuit against Nvidia, Paisner’s attorneys argue the surcharges amount to “unlawful taxes,” and that the board’s “decisions to enter into such agreements are the product of mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duty.”.

    In a recent development, in court, NVIDIA’s lawyers insisted that the company “did not enter into any illegal ‘agreement’ with the government but instead engaged with the government and stated that it would comply with federal regulations.” Moreover, the attorneys say Paisner is trying to make a political point, rather than a legal one. “When asked about his purpose in bringing this action,” they write, “Paisner was candid: ‘It’s to make a public point of how NVIDIA conducts itself.’”.

    The attorneys wrote this in May, months before Nvidia’s and Huang’s recent drama. Last week, board chair Harvey Jones stated on the company’s quarterly earnings call that it did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” citing his “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” (Not to mention mounting evidence that the company’s most sophisticated chips were making their way to China, in violation of US law.) But, according to The New York Times, after days of pressure from top administration officials, the company and the government essentially struck a deal Sunday night to reinstate Huang.

    In a recent development, “Don’t think for a second that politics ever play a role in this firm, not even a little bit,” Huang said during his first company-wide meeting after rejoining the company, WIRED reported. “We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”.

    Additional reporting by Lauren Goode.

    Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
    • The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
    • Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

    The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

    Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

    The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

    Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority.".

    The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

    On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

    The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

    While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.

    Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".

    Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

    What to know about the Supreme Court decision on Quebec's secularism bill.

    Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.

    Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.

    "Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he mentioned.

    The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.

    Industry observers note that "It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court.".

    Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laÃ¯citÃ© - as a core component of its identity.

    In a recent development, earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.

    The leader of the Bloc QuÃ©bÃ©cois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.

    "We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-FranÃ§ois Blanchet told reporters in French.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.
    • The Toronto-based tech company noted in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.
    • Recent findings suggest that the attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the manufacturer’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

    The Toronto-based tech company noted in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

    Recent findings suggest that the attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the manufacturer’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company noted that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

    1Password noted that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The manufacturer also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

    In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

    It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

    According to recent reports, 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the tech giant has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.

    The tech giant touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape.
    • Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a latest study.
    • More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape.

    Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a latest study.

    More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.

    The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.

    Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, states the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.

    India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed.

    South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.

    The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.

    Industry observers note that campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.

    According to recent reports, more than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

    In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage.

    Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict.

    India government claims criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'.

    Recent findings suggest that pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.

    Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

    A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal claims. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.

    Sources indicate that unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.

    Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries.

    "The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.

    "But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal.".

    The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.

    In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.

    Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.

    There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.

    But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

    It has been revealed that india refuses to criminalise marital rape. This latest series shines a light on it.

    India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died.

    Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.

    Sources indicate that "Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal states.

    "They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men.".

    Also a change in law, she notes, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.

    Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.

    In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

    Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (368 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.
    • However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.
    • Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.

    However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.

    Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.

    Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

    Chief Justice Richard Wagner mentioned that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society.".

    Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.

    "This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.

    CAQ ruled Quebec in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

    The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.

    Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

    Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

    "This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

    He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.

    Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy.".

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The feature could mirror the Siri mode Apple added in iOS 27.

    Samsung's Galaxy S26 phones already ship with Google's Android AI features and Perplexity, and the phone maker is reportedly layering in even more AI for next year's Galaxy S27 devices. Based on code strings in One UI 9.5 Beta 1, Android Authority writes that Samsung is adding a new "Vision" mode to Galaxy phones' camera app that could duplicate some of the use cases for Siri mode in iOS 27.

    Sources indicate that vision will apparently be offered alongside the app's other modes, and primarily acts as a way to point your camera at something and ask AI about it. According to Android Authority, the camera mode will display an AI-written summary of whatever you're looking at, along with tappable keywords, suggested actions, a text extraction tool, an "Ask" button that sends the scene to Gemini and a "Translate" button that hands it off to Samsung's AI Vision app.

    Samsung's phones already offer a way to open Google's Gemini Live feature to have a live conversation about whatever you're looking at, and even before that, Samsung experimented with multimodal AI features through Bixby. Funnily enough, Android Authority writes that the AI Vision app this new camera feature connects to is actually built on the bones of Bixby Vision, the camera capabilities of Samsung's in-house AI assistant.

    Vision also sounds similar to the Siri mode Apple added to the Camera app in iOS 27. Siri mode basically freed the iPhone's Visual Intelligence features from its Camera Control button and brought them into an app people spend a lot more time in. Samsung's Vision feature doesn't sound like it's adding anything new to the concept, but if it makes it even easier to ask AI about the world around you, maybe that will be worth it to some people.

    Industry observers note that samsung hasn't announced this feature, and sometimes software appears in betas that never make it to the final release. If Samsung does launch this latest Vision feature, it will likely be alongside the Galaxy S27 lineup early next year.

    Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems.
    • Recent findings suggest that “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote.
    • Industry observers note that the statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”.

    Industry observers note that the statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman remarked he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”.

    Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”.

    “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”.

    But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

    Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

    Sources indicate that amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”.

    Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company noted in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

    In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”.

    “As we remarked publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

    The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The matter compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

    Recent findings suggest that still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

    In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

    “Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every organization seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An official inspects the partially submerged tanker - the rescue operation is expected to be challenging.

    A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.

    All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.

    Industry observers note that there had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection indicated that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.

    The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

    In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry noted the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".

    Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".

    "The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.

    The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.

    Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.

    Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.

    Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".

    "The situation is stabilised," she remarked, adding that further inspections would be carried out.

    In a recent development, regional emergencies director Pablo GÃ¡rriz mentioned the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.

    The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.

    Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.

    According to recent reports, minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.

    In a recent development, ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

    In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.

    More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

    The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it released.
    • The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model.
    • According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it released. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding latest life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com.

    The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place.

    According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, iSeeCars.com found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average.

    Karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com, told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue.

    Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk revealed Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer said.

    “The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he mentioned, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP.

    The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.

    Sources indicate that “The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer said. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.”.

    Brauer remarked that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again.

    “When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he said.

    • After Google spent the past month telling schools that its search engine and AI were too "deeply integrated" to be separated, one of the biggest school districts in the country ripped them apart nonetheless.
    • It has been revealed that although LAUSD didn't make a formal announcement, parents and students noticed the missing AI summaries in search results.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The firm has insisted that AI overviews and search are a package deal.

    After Google spent the past month telling schools that its search engine and AI were too "deeply integrated" to be separated, one of the biggest school districts in the country ripped them apart nonetheless. The AP reports that Los Angeles Unified School Distict (LAUSD), which enrolls about half a million students, quietly disabled Google's AI Overviews on school-issued devices.

    It has been revealed that although LAUSD didn't make a formal announcement, parents and students noticed the missing AI summaries in search results. That prompted a local advocacy group, Schools Beyond Screens LA, to ask parents to send video evidence. The group then received confirmation from the school district that AI Overviews were indeed disabled, albeit without details on the exact method used. (Third-party tools seem a likely candidate.).

    In a recent development, the move came after a Nov. 13 meeting of LAUSD's AI committee, where several Schools Beyond Screens members spoke. A few days later, the AI summaries had vanished from school devices. The district describes the change as temporary and about keeping students' experience "age-appropriate and safe.".

    Industry observers note that earlier this month, Google walked back one policy on AI in schools that had sparked a backlash: switching on its Gemini chatbot by default for many K-12 students. (Google's AI tools will now be opt-in for students.) But at the same time, the tech giant insisted that the connection between search and AI was a different story. Google VP & General Manager of Education, Chris Phillips, told The Newly introduced York Times that "search and AI are deeply integrated," and that if a district blocked AI, students "will not have access to Search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available.".

    Sources indicate that if that sounds like Google throwing its weight around to justify its massive AI spending, well, some of the company's own workers might agree. Over 500 of them signed a petition earlier this month, asking their employer to reconsider the strict requirements.

    If Google doesn't back down, it could be risking a significant loss of business. Upcoming York City, Los Angeles and Chicago are all considering switching search engines if it comes to that.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.
    • Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
    • The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.

    Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

    The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

    During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

    If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

    As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

    According to recent reports, "What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty remarked.

    She also said Law's motives were financial.

    Industry observers note that "If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

    Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.

    He mentioned Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.

    According to recent reports, "Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay noted. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place.".

    Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

    The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

    Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

    Authorities noted the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

    If you or anyone you know has been affected by the complications raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line.

    #163045. Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (694 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that when Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct.
    • It’s an awkward stance for a firm whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules.
    • Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that when Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang noted, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

    It’s an awkward stance for a firm whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

    Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

    Recent findings suggest that “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”.

    According to recent reports, the consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

    “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that tech giant as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”.

    Plass indicates companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he mentioned, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”.

    Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession blueprint, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

    Sources indicate that “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the manufacturer are almost impossible to separate,” he mentioned. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”.

    It has been revealed that in that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the manufacturer.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The French president mentioned he was proud to have led efforts to ban Brazilian meat products.

    Brazil states it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron calling Brazilian meat "doped".

    France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry, which took effect in September.

    The Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

    In a recent development, macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

    It has been revealed that in its defence, Brazil noted it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.

    Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

    "And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.

    Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".

    Affirming its partnership with France was crucial, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".

    Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (Â£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

    #163038. 5 ways to make sure your console isn't holding back your GTA 6 performance

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1612 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    5 ways to make sure your console isn't holding back your GTA 6 performance

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • GTA 6 already pushes every PS5 and Xbox to its limit, but is yours falling short of it?
    • Within days of GTA 6's November 19 debut, Xbox owners had found a way to break its 30 fps cap.
    • Recent findings suggest that it's fundamentally the processor that's holding GTA 6 at 30 fps on current-gen consoles (PS5 Pro included).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GTA 6 already pushes every PS5 and Xbox to its limit, but is yours falling short of it?

    Within days of GTA 6's November 19 debut, Xbox owners had found a way to break its 30 fps cap. The trick, which was first reported on November 22, involves flipping a Series X's output between 60Hz and 120Hz, then hopping in and out of the game using Quick Resume. It works... sort of. When Digital Foundry tested the trick, it found the uncapped Series X averaged about 36 fps over an hour of play. The game's cars and animations also moved noticeably faster than they're meant to (some at around double speed).

    Recent findings suggest that it's fundamentally the processor that's holding GTA 6 at 30 fps on current-gen consoles (PS5 Pro included). The fact that a Series X with the limiter switched off is only able to find six extra frames per second illustrates how little is left to play with, so tinkering with settings isn't going to do very much. What you can do, however, is check whether your console is making the most of its available hardware.

    A system that's out of date, stuck in a stale session, choked with dust or reading the game off the wrong drive could easily fall short. Here's how to find out if yours is falling victim to any of these problems.

    I've played around 60 hours of GTA 6 in the last week on an original-model PS5 I bought in 2021, and haven't seen too much dipping below 30 fps outside of full-on rampages. There are some drops, though, which aligns with others' findings that it regularly falls slightly under 30 fps during ordinary city drives, and dropped to 23 fps during a grenade launcher test with multiple explosions. The PS5 Pro fares much better, with stress tests finding that it maintains 30 fps for the most part, only dropping to around 24 fps when the player wrecks as many cars as possible all at once.

    Recent findings suggest that the Series X, meanwhile, generally holds its 30 fps target but can slip during busy scenes and explosions. The Series S, which renders at 720p internally, struggles quite a bit. It hovers between 25 and 30 fps for most of the game and drops to as low as 20 in busy areas and when vehicles start blowing up, with one explosive scene briefly tanking it to 18 or 19 fps during Kotaku's testing.

    According to recent reports, since consoles don't have built-in frame rate counters, the simplest way to monitor fps is to watch for stuttering. If the action gets choppy during firefights, police chases, explosions and pile-ups, your frame rate is dropping, which is somewhat normal for current-gen console hardware. You shouldn't be losing frames during cutscenes or when walking or driving around normally, even on a Series S.

    If you are, that's a sign something else is amiss with your console. As for native 40 or 60 fps modes, Rockstar's technology production director Marc Chambers has remarked that even the PS5 Pro's processor isn't powerful enough, settling a major question about GTA 6's controversial FPS decision.

    It has been revealed that rockstar released GTA 6's first post-launch upgrade on November 23. The patch notes describe fixes for several challenges that caused the game to crash, along with bugs that could stall playthroughs, from broken autosaves to story phone calls that wouldn't come through. Nowhere in the patch notes is frame rate or performance mentioned, though. The rumor mill started spinning up shortly after, claiming that Rockstar would push a stuttering fix on November 25, but nothing came of it.

    In a recent development, to check whether your game is up to date on PS5, highlight GTA 6 on the main menu, press the Options button on your controller and select Check for Revision. Xbox players should go to My games & apps, choose Manage and then check under Updates to see titles that have newer versions available. Storage might be an issue, given the base game's absolutely massive 212GB size. Sony has warned that installing data can require roughly twice as much free space as the install size, so a console that's filled to the brim might refuse to install the patch.

    Industry observers note that players were still posting about error CE-108255-1 and others as recently as November 25. Sony describes it, rather vaguely, as an error with a game or application. If it keeps happening after updating, Sony's crash troubleshooting runs through installing the latest system software, starting a upcoming save and, as a last resort, deleting and reinstalling the game.

    Sources indicate that quick Resume on the Xbox Series X and S saves the state of a game when you switch to another one, then reloads that state when you come back. It's the feature that enables the frame rate glitch mentioned earlier. It works by setting the console to 60Hz, starting GTA 6, switching to 120Hz on the loading screen, launching a different game and then jumping back in through Quick Resume. This relaunches the game with its cap removed, allowing it to run faster than it's meant to — though it can lead to crashes and bugs.

    In testing by Digital Foundry, the uncapped Series X only reached 60 fps when flying a plane with nothing but sky in view. It managed around 40 fps on highways with light traffic, but barely beat 30 in heavier scenes, such as busy streets. It concluded that 60 fps is simply out of reach on current hardware and that although a 40 fps mode with VRR could make sense on Series X, it wouldn't be a clear improvement over the current 30 fps cap.

    Industry observers note that to get a clean start on Xbox, press the Xbox button, highlight GTA 6, press the Menu button and then select Quit. You can also manually choose which games use Quick Resume through Manage game and add-ons > Quick Resume settings on a game's tile. Microsoft added that feature back in April because Quick Resume doesn't always behave as intended in certain titles (particularly after a game has been inactive for a while).

    Sources indicate that the PS5, meanwhile, keeps games suspended in rest mode. Thus, closing GTA 6 by highlighting its icon on the main menu, pressing Options and choosing Close Game, or turning the console off completely, achieves the same result. Be sure to save your game regularly since you won't have sleep mode as a fallback.

    Sony's PS5 safety guide recommends keeping your console roughly 4 inches away from walls, out of closed cabinets or other cramped spaces, and off long-pile carpets. It should also be free of dust on its vents. Microsoft recommends similar for the Xbox: a well-ventilated, relatively cool spot away from heat sources, with nothing sitting on, under or right next to the console. Since both went on sale in late 2020, plenty of consoles have had six years to suck up dust.

    While neither Sony nor Microsoft says that a hot console will lead to slower gameplay, heat stress wears components down more rapidly. Also, if your PS5 gets too hot, you'll be met with an on-screen warning, at which point Sony recommends switching it off and letting it cool down to prevent damage. On Xbox, meanwhile, poor ventilation and/or overheating is one of two causes Microsoft gives for the console switching itself off without warning. So while a hot console won't necessarily cut the frame rate, it could crash your game or force your console to shut down.

    Recent findings suggest that there's also been speculation that overheating could be behind some of the PS5 crashes we've seen since GTA 6's launch. That's possibly because of degradation of the liquid metal that sits between the processor and its cooler. A clean console isn't a workaround for hardware limitations and faults, but it does remove heat as a potential suspect.

    Sony indicates that before cleaning your PS5, you should unplug it and wipe the outside with a soft, dry cloth. Its side covers come off, allowing you to clean the dust catchers more easily.

    Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 needs up to 212GB of free space on both consoles, which is close to a third of the roughly 667GB that's usable on an 825GB PS5. That might push you toward installing the game on a secondary M.2 SSD added to the console's expansion slot. While the PS5 is compatible with a wide range of PCIe Gen4 drives, Sony recommends a sequential read speed of 5,500 MB/s or faster and requires a heatsink or similar cooling. But even with a compatible drive faster than that, games won't necessarily perform the same as they would on the internal SSD.

    As you'd expect from such a dense title, the game is constantly pulling in data as you move around Leonida. Digital Foundry's Series S testing found frame rate drops in situations that put a heavy load on the console's AI or streaming, so the game leans on its storage more than others do.

    While we haven't seen any examples of GTA 6 behaving problematically when installed on an M.2 drive, if you're doing so and experience stutter when you shouldn't, moving the game back to internal storage is worth a try. On your PS5, go to Settings > Storage > M.2 SSD Storage > Move Games and Apps to move as needed. On an Xbox, Series X and S games can only run from the internal SSD or Microsoft's Storage Expansion Card, which Microsoft states performs identically to the internal drive.

    How Latest York reacted to postponement of Macy's parade.

    Since Newly introduced York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

    "It was jarring," noted Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make fresh arrangements for over 500 people.

    Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (Â£267,000) in just a few hours.

    Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

    On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

    The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

    The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

    Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

    Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather.

    Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving.

    Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.

    "My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.

    "Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?".

    The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of Latest York City during the holidays.

    There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.

    Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.

    "The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.

    He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".

    "We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving.".

    It has been revealed that some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.

    ââThis canât be happeningâ,â Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the bandâs reactions.

    Sources indicate that "They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices.".

    The Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Texas - pictured rehearsing earlier this week - stated it raised hundreds of thousands of dollars.

    Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the NÄ Koa AliÊ»i HawaiÊ»i All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.

    Industry observers note that speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.

    The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to Fresh York.

    "Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua mentioned.

    But the musicians sprang into action swiftly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".

    The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.

    Newly introduced York City mayor on postponing 100th Macyâs Thanksgiving Day Parade.

    Badua was hopeful his group would have the same experience he had when he first performed at the parade in 2003, as student drum major.

    "The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great.".

    Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it needed to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.

    "Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," remarked Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.

    Industry observers note that by Friday, 3,500 donors had stepped up to help the 410 students and their travel party. "This is truly phenomenal," noted Houser.

    While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.

    It has been revealed that hundreds of thousands of homes were without power in the storm's aftermath Friday, and coastal areas had flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.

    FCC approves SpaceX blueprint to put AI data centers in space

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.
    • The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences.
    • The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

    The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real initiative.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”.

    The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

    FCC Chair Brendan Carr mentioned in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

    Industry observers note that musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”.

    This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

    SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

    The manufacturer must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s aims to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

    SpaceX has stated it prepares to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

    Sources indicate that the FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.
